newsitem.title: USA: Fed raises key interest rate by quarter-point.
newsitem.headline: Fed raises key interest rate by quarter-point.

text.p: The U.S. Federal Reserve on Tuesday raised interest rates for the first time in over two years in an effort to stay a step ahead of inflation and keep the economic expansion on track.

The quarter-percentage-point increase brought the federal funds rate that commercial banks charge each other for overnight loans up to 5.50 percent. The Fed left the discount rate it charges banks for money unchanged at 5.0 percent.

"This action was taken in light of persisting strength in demand, which is progressively increasing the risk of inflationary imbalances developing in the economy that would eventually undermine the long expansion," the Fed said in a statement.
The rate increase, the first since February 1995, is likely to lead to higher borrowing costs for many consumers and companies, from credit card users to the stores they shop at.

The Fed's move had been widely expected on Wall Street, but it is nevertheless expected to draw fire on Capitol Hill, where lawmakers have already questioned why the central bank was even considering raising rates when inflation was so low.
Tuesday's rate increase marked a reversal of Fed policy. Its last rate change came on January 31, 1996, when it trimmed rates by a quarter percentage point.

"The slight firming of monetary conditions is viewed as a prudent step that affords greater assurance of prolonging the current economic expansion by sustaining the existing low-inflation environment through the rest of this year and next," the Fed said.
"The experience of the last several years has reinforced the conviction that low inflation is essential to realizing the economy's fullest growth potential," it added.

Analysts are divided over the Fed's next move. Many believe that central bank policymakers will raise rates at least one more time, possibly as soon as their next meeting on May 20, to slow down the economy and head off inflation.
But others are not so sure and argue that the economy will cool off on its own without any further action by the Fed.

After expanding at a brisk 3.9 percent annualized pace in the fourth quarter of last year, the economy looks to have slowed slightly in the first three months of this year to a growth rate closer to three percent, analysts said.
Much of the slowdown has occured in the so-called external sector, as U.S. exports have sagged and imports have soared, in part because the strong dollar has made foreign goods cheaper.

Domestic U.S. demand has stayed strong, although special factors may have played a role. This winter has been much milder than last, spurring construction, and consumer spending has been boosted by larger-than-normal tax refunds.
Greenspan told lawmakers last week that the economy retains a "great deal of vigor" and termed the prospects for a continuation of the six-year-old expansion "quite favorable."
But he also made clear that that depended critically on the Fed staying ahead of inflation and keeping it from rising.

"If we allow that to get away, we will at the end of the day find that we have set in motion a set of forces which bring the long, sustainable, stable recovery to an end," he told the Congressional Joint Economic Committee last week.

In response to repeated questioning by lawmakers, Greenspan acknowledged that inflation has remained low, but he argued that the Fed needed to look ahead and anticipate price pressures in the future that could derail the economy.
He pointed to the tight jobs market in particular as a potential source of concern, voicing worries that it could lead to excessive wage demands and spiralling inflation.
Greenspan has also singled out the buoyant stock market for attention. The Fed is worried that equity prices may have risen too far and may be a harbinger of higher inflation ahead.
